"Look at him go again!" Clara whispered, peering through the slats of the boathouse window. "That's the third morning in a row."

Out on the misty surface of Eagle Lake, a lone figure in a small rowboat moved steadily toward the far shore. He was a new guest at the lakeside inn, a stern man named Mr. Finch who spoke to no one.

"He's just an early riser, Clara," Alice replied, stifling a yawn. "Some people like to fish before breakfast."

"Fish? He never has a pole, or a tackle box, or even a net! All he ever carries is that strange leather satchel."

"Maybe he just enjoys the exercise," Alice reasoned. "The doctor told my father he needed more of it."

"I'll bet a dollar he's no fisherman!" Clara declared. "He's mapping the lake floor. I heard the manager say Mr. Finch was some kind of engineer."

"So? Why would he map the lake floor in secret, at five in the morning?"

"Because he's a saboteur!" Clara announced with a dramatic flourish. "Everyone knows the new power plant is being built just downriver. He's probably looking for a weak spot in the bedrock to plant explosives!"

Alice giggled. "Honestly, Clara, your imagination is working overtime again. Yesterday you were certain the headwaiter was a jewel thief."

"Well, he does have shifty eyes. But this is different. This feels real."

"Then you have no interest in getting some of the chef's famous blueberry pancakes before they're all gone?"

"Of course I do! I just don't believe Mr. Finch is an honest engineer."

"Quiet!" Alice hissed suddenly. "He's coming back!"

The rowboat was indeed approaching the dock. The girls ducked lower, watching as Mr. Finch tied the rope to a cleat with practiced efficiency. He stepped onto the dock, the leather satchel clutched tightly in one hand. He paused for a moment, scanning the shoreline. His eyes seemed to linger on the boathouse, and both girls held their breath. Then, with a shrug, he turned and walked briskly up the path toward the inn.

"You see," Clara whispered fiercely once he was out of sight. "He looked right at us! He's suspicious!"

"Or he heard us whispering," Alice countered. "Come on. Pancakes."

They were halfway through their breakfast when Mr. Finch entered the dining room. He stopped at their table.

"Good morning, young ladies," he said, his voice a low rumble. "Enjoying the lake?"

"Yes, sir," Clara managed, her mouth full of pancake.

"It's a fine body of water," Mr. Finch continued, his gaze sharp. "One must be careful, though. The currents can be tricky, especially if one doesn't know what they're doing. It would be a shame if anyone got into trouble." With a curt nod, he moved on to a private table in the corner.

The question caught them both by surprise. Clara felt her face flush.

"I guess he scored a point on you that time," Alice murmured. "He knows we were watching him."

"So we made him nervous!"

"You needn't sound so pleased about it."

"But it's all so peculiar. Why warn us about currents? Why be so mysterious?" Clara insisted. "I'll leave the detective work to you. For now, I'm going to finish my breakfast."

"How do we know he was just warning us?" Clara speculated. "Maybe it was a threat! Maybe he's on to us and wants us to stop watching!"

"That's so!" Alice acknowledged, her eyes widening. "He didn't sound very friendly."

"If he were just a harmless engineer, he would have been amused by a couple of curious girls," Clara reasoned. "Instead, he tried to frighten us away. He's definitely hiding something."

"You think he really has something dangerous in that satchel?"

"That's my theory, Alice. And I'm going to find out what it is." Restlessly, Clara stared out the window at the now sunlit lake. A delivery truck was pulling up the long gravel driveway, kicking up dust. A man in a work uniform hopped out, carrying a small, heavy-looking crate.

"Wait a minute!" Clara exclaimed, pointing. "Look!"

Alice followed her gaze. The delivery man was walking not to the inn's main entrance, but toward the corner table where Mr. Finch sat alone. The two men spoke for a moment, their heads close together. Mr. Finch nodded, slid a thick envelope across the table, and the delivery man quickly pocketed it before leaving the crate by the side of the table. He was back in his truck and roaring down the driveway in less than a minute.

"He didn't even get a signature!" Alice gasped.

"Of course not! It wasn't an official delivery!" Clara said, her eyes shining with excitement. "That was the exchange!"

"Exchange for what?"

"I don't know yet," Clara admitted, leaping to her feet. "But I think we just found the answer to a few of our questions."

"The question of what a supposed geological engineer is doing with a mysterious crate delivered by a man who doesn't wait for a signature!" Mr. Finch, oblivious to the intense scrutiny from the girls' table, calmly finished his coffee. He then gestured to a young, lanky porter who was clearing a nearby table. The porter, a boy of about seventeen with a perpetually cheerful expression, hurried over. Mr. Finch spoke to him in a low tone, pointing to the crate. The porter, whose name was Tom, nodded eagerly. He hoisted the heavy crate, grunting with the effort, and began to carry it not toward the elevators or the guest rooms, but toward a side door that led out the back of the inn. "He's not taking it to his room," Clara observed, her voice barely a breath. "Where could he be going with it?" "Maybe to a storage closet," Alice suggested, though her tone lacked conviction. "No, this is something else. He needs a special place for it. Come on!" Clara slid from her chair, leaving her half-eaten pancakes behind. "But my breakfast!" Alice protested weakly. "We can eat later! We can't lose him!" Clara insisted, already moving toward the lobby. Alice sighed, dabbed her mouth with a napkin, and hurried to catch up. They reached the inn's wide, wrap-around veranda just in time to see Tom disappearing down a shaded path that led away from the main building. The path wound through a manicured garden before branching off toward a cluster of smaller, older outbuildings. "He's heading for the old ice house!" Clara declared. "Why on earth would he take it there?" "To keep it cool?" Alice offered. "Mr. Finch told the front desk his equipment was sensitive to heat." "Sensitive equipment or a secret that he wants to keep on ice," Clara countered. "I'll bet another cookie that whatever is in that crate, he doesn't want anyone from the inn to stumble across it." The girls waited until Tom had deposited the crate and was heading back toward the inn before they ventured down the path. The ice house was a curious structure, built halfway into the side of a grassy knoll. It had thick stone walls, a heavy wooden door bound with iron straps, and no windows. A large, formidable-looking padlock secured the door. "Well, that's that," Alice said with an air of finality. "We can't get in." "Not now, maybe," Clara said, her eyes scanning the area. "But Mr. Finch will have to come back for it. And when he does, we'll be watching." They spent the rest of the day in a state of restless anticipation. Clara found it impossible to concentrate on the book she had brought, her gaze constantly straying to the path leading to the ice house. Alice, while trying to appear calm, kept jumping at every sound. They took their lunch on the veranda, positioning their table for a clear view. Mr. Finch appeared only once, striding down to the lake with a fishing rod. He seemed the very picture of a vacationing sportsman. "You see?" Louise said. "He's just fishing. Maybe you're making this all up in your head." "A man can fish and still be a spy," Clara retorted stubbornly. "He's just trying to look innocent. He knows we're watching him." As dusk began to settle over the lake, painting the sky in shades of orange and purple, their patience was rewarded. Mr. Finch emerged from the inn. He carried no fishing rod this time. He glanced around the veranda, his sharp eyes sweeping the area, and then walked with purpose down the path to the ice house. The girls ducked behind a large lilac bush, their hearts thumping. From their hiding place, they saw him produce a key, unlock the heavy padlock, and slip inside, closing the thick door behind him. "Now what?" Alice whispered after several long minutes of silence. "We wait," Clara breathed. The minutes stretched into what felt like an hour. The last of the sunlight faded, and the air grew cool. From within the stone building, they began to hear a faint, rhythmic noise. It was a soft but distinct tapping. Tap-tap-tap. Pause. Tappity-tap. "What is that?" Alice whispered, moving closer to Clara. "It sounds like a woodpecker." "There are no woodpeckers in a stone house," Clara said, her mind racing. "It's a sound. A signal. He's doing something in there." They strained to listen, but the sound was too muffled to decipher. It continued intermittently for another twenty minutes before the door creaked open. Mr. Finch stepped out, relocked the padlock, and walked back to the inn without a backward glance. "He was in there for nearly an hour," Alice marveled. "Just making that tapping noise." "It has to be the answer to the whole puzzle," Clara declared, her excitement overriding her fear. "But we need to know what's in that crate, and what's making that sound." Their chance to investigate further was interrupted by a new voice. "Hiding from the mosquitos?" A young man with sandy hair and a friendly smile had come up the path behind them. He was carrying a pair of binoculars and a small notebook. The girls jumped, startled. "We were just… admiring the garden," Clara stammered. "It's a bit late for that," the young man said with a good-natured chuckle. "I'm Ben, by the way. I work for the university, studying the local warbler population." "I'm Clara, and this is my friend Alice," Clara said, deciding in an instant to take a risk. "We're not really looking at the garden. We're investigating a mystery." Alice shot her a look of pure panic, but Clara ignored it. She quickly explained their suspicions about Mr. Finch, the hidden satchel, the secret delivery of the crate, and the strange tapping noises from the ice house. Ben listened intently, his cheerful demeanor giving way to a more serious expression. "Tapping, you say?" he asked when she had finished. "Rhythmic, like a code?" "Exactly!" Clara said. "Alice thought it was a woodpecker." "I'm an amateur radio operator," Ben said thoughtfully. "A ham radio enthusiast. That sound… it could be someone practicing Morse code on a telegraph key. But to do that, you'd need a transmitter." "A what?" Alice asked. "A radio," Ben explained. "Something to send signals. Did you say the crate he received was heavy?" "Yes, the porter could barely lift it," Clara confirmed. Ben's eyes lit up with understanding. "And he put it in the ice house. That would be a perfect place. The thick stone walls would muffle the sound and help hide any radio waves from casual detection. And it's isolated." "So you think he's a spy, too?" Clara asked eagerly. "I think," Ben said slowly, "that a man who hides things in boathouses and operates a secret radio from an ice house is certainly not a geological engineer on vacation. I think you girls have stumbled onto something very serious." The next afternoon, their opportunity arrived. They watched from the lobby as Mr. Finch got into his car and drove away from the inn, heading toward the main highway. "This is our chance!" Clara whispered to Ben, who was pretending to read a newspaper nearby. "He'll be gone for at least an hour." Alice, though nervous, was now too deep in the mystery to back out. The three of them slipped out the back and hurried to the ice house. "Now for the lock," Clara said, looking at the formidable padlock. Ben grinned. "Leave that to me." He pulled a small leather case from his pocket. It contained a set of thin metal picks. "A hobby of mine," he explained as he knelt by the door. "Good for getting into old sheds and things when you forget your keys." With a surprising dexterity, he worked at the lock. After a tense minute, there was a satisfying click. The padlock sprang open. "You're a lifesaver, Ben!" Clara exclaimed. Ben pushed the heavy door inward, revealing a dark, musty interior. The air that wafted out was cold and smelled of damp earth and sawdust. Taking a deep breath, they stepped inside, pulling the door partially closed behind them so as not to be seen. In the center of the room sat the crate. The lid had been pried off and was set to one side. Clara, Alice, and Ben peered inside. It was not filled with survey equipment. Instead, it was packed with a complex assortment of electronic components: vacuum tubes, coiled copper wires, a panel of black dials, and a large, heavy battery. A set of headphones and a small microphone lay on a bed of excelsior. And there, connected by a wire to the main apparatus, was a small, brass telegraph key. "It's a short wave transmitter," Ben breathed, his voice filled with awe. "And a powerful one. This is military grade, or close to it." Clara's eyes scanned the small, cluttered space. On a small wooden ledge next to the crate, she spotted a notepad. She picked it up. The top page was filled with columns of letters and numbers. "Look at this," she said, showing it to the others. "It looks like a code." Ben examined the page. "It certainly is. See this here? B4. That's likely a call sign. A name for the person sending or receiving the message." "B4," Clara repeated thoughtfully. "And these other numbers must be the message itself." "We need to get this to the police," Alice said, her voice trembling slightly. "Not yet," Ben countered. "They might not believe us. A local sheriff might just think it's a ham radio operator who hasn't paid his license fee. We need more. We need to know what he's transmitting." Suddenly, from outside, they heard the crunch of gravel. A car engine. "He's back!" Alice gasped. "He came back early!" Panic seized them. They had to get out, but they couldn't be seen. "The crate!" Clara hissed. "Make it look like we were never here!" Ben quickly but carefully placed the notepad back on the ledge. In his haste, he nudged a small screwdriver, which rolled off the ledge and fell silently into the thick sawdust on the floor. There was no time to look for it. They scrambled out of the ice house, Ben quickly snapping the padlock shut just as Mr. Finch's car came into view around a bend in the driveway. They dove into the same lilac bush as before, their hearts hammering against their ribs. Mr. Finch parked his car and walked directly to the ice house. He paused at the door, his hand on the padlock. For one terrifying moment, the girls were certain he was checking it, that he knew. He seemed to scan the ground, his brow furrowed. Then, with a slight shrug, he unlocked it and went inside. "He didn't see us," Alice whispered, letting out a shaky breath. "But that was too close." "He knows something's wrong," Clara said grimly. "I saw the way he looked at the lock. And Ben, you dropped a screwdriver." "I know," Ben said, his face pale. "He'll find it. He'll know someone was in there." "Which means he'll be on his guard," Clara reasoned. "And he'll probably move whatever is in that satchel. We have to get to the boathouse. Now. It's our last chance." They decided on a desperate plan. Ben, being the fastest runner, would create a diversion on the far side of the inn. He would start shouting about a rare bird he had spotted, a tactic sure to draw the attention of the other guests and, hopefully, distract Mr. Finch if he came out of the ice house. Meanwhile, Clara and Alice would race to the boathouse. They waited five minutes, then heard Ben's voice from across the lawn. "A cerulean warbler! Over here! I can't believe it!" Guests on the veranda stood up, murmuring and looking toward the woods where Ben was pointing frantically. It was the distraction they needed. "Go!" Clara urged Alice. They ran, low and fast, across the lawn to the path that led down to the lake. The boathouse was quiet, the water lapping gently against its wooden pilings. They slipped inside, the familiar smell of lake water and old wood greeting them. "The floorboard is over here," Clara whispered, heading for the corner where Mr. Finch had knelt. She found the board with the odd notch and, using her fingernails, pried it up. There, nestled in the dark space below, was the leather satchel. It was surprisingly heavy. With trembling hands, Clara lifted it out. "Open it," Alice urged, keeping a nervous watch on the door. Clara fumbled with the brass clasps. They sprang open. She lifted the leather flap. Inside were not papers, or maps, or stolen jewels. The satchel was filled with thick, intricately carved steel plates. Each one bore the reverse image of a complex design, like a piece of a puzzle. "What are they?" Alice asked in confusion. "They look like stamps." "They're dies," Clara said, her voice a low murmur of discovery. "For printing, or minting. This one… it looks like the edge of a twenty dollar bill." At that moment, a dark shadow fell across the boathouse entrance. The door creaked open. Mr. Finch stood there, his large frame filling the doorway. His suit was immaculate, but his face was like a thundercloud. He had not been fooled by the diversion. "I believe," he said, his voice a low and dangerous rumble, "you have something that belongs to me." The girls were frozen in terror. There was nowhere to run. Mr. Finch took a slow step into the boathouse, his eyes fixed on the open satchel in Clara's hands. "That was very foolish, girls," he continued, his voice devoid of any warmth. "Very foolish indeed. I warned you to be careful of the currents."

"The potted palms," she whispered.

"What was that, miss?" the officer asked.

"On the veranda," Penny said, her voice growing stronger. "When Mrs. Deline was watching us. She was sitting on the veranda. And when we left, we walked behind a potted palm to get away from her."

"What about it?" Louise asked, confused.

He thought she had the code. He locked her in there and went after us. She used a miniature emergency transmitter to send the Morse code signal."

Mrs. Deline, her white suit now smudged with dirt, looked at Penny with a new respect. "Your theory was correct, Penny. I am working with the government. I was assigned to watch Jim McCoy at the lighthouse. We suspected he was receiving information, but we didn't know how. The 'fish bones' I buried were actually a tracking device I was attempting to plant near a pre-arranged drop spot."

"Then Jim McCoy is B4?" Louise asked.

"No!" the radio officer interrupted. "Sir, the broadcast! We got a fix. It's coming from the hotel roof!"

Jerry and Mrs. Deline stared at him in disbelief.

"The hotel?" Jerry repeated. "Then McCoy isn't the broadcaster."

"No," Mrs. Deline said slowly, a look of dawning horror on her face. "McCoy isn't the broadcaster. He's the courier. He gets information from ships offshore and passes it along. But he wouldn't know how to operate a short wave radio. He's just a disgruntled old sailor." She turned to Jerry. "There's only one other person who had access to both the lighthouse and the hotel. One person who helped McCoy with his duties, who came and went as he pleased, who was friendly with all the staff at the Crystal Inn."

Penny knew the answer before Mrs. Deline even said the name. It was the man who was always helpful, always offhanded, always in a hurry. The man who had taken them to the monitoring truck in the first place.

"Jerry," Penny said, her voice barely a whisper. "When we came to the truck, you introduced us to the officers. But there was someone else. The man who came out to salute you."

"Corporal Evans," Jerry said, turning to the soldier beside him.

But it was not Corporal Evans. The man who stood there, a faint, cruel smile on his face, was the same man Penny remembered. And in his hand, he was no longer holding a rifle. He was holding a small, black pistol, and it was pointed directly at Jerry Livingston.

"The real Corporal Evans is tied up in the woods," the man said calmly. "It was quite simple to take his place two days ago. You government men are so trusting." He gestured with the pistol. "Now, Agent Livingston, I will take the code you are carrying. And you, Mrs. Deline, your little game is over."

It was Finch. He had shed his bulky coat and hat, put on a uniform, and simply walked into their midst. The chase in the cave had all been a distraction, a way to keep Jerry and the girls occupied while he made his move.

"You're B4," Jerry stated, not moving a muscle.

"For all the good it will do you to know," Finch sneered. "I am. And my associate is at the hotel, preparing to move the equipment. That last broadcast was a warning to him that you were getting too close. A warning he unfortunately did not receive, as he is no doubt in custody by now." He shrugged. "No matter. There are other radios. But that code contains the locations of a dozen escape routes. I will have it."

He took a step toward Jerry. But he had forgotten about the two girls. In that split second, Louise, who was closest to the truck's heavy metal door, acted on pure instinct. With a cry, she swung the door with all her might. It slammed into Finch's side, knocking him off balance. The pistol fired, the shot going wild and shattering one of the truck's windows.

At the same time, Penny grabbed the heavy map board from the table and brought it down hard on Finch's outstretched arm. The pistol clattered to the floor. Before Finch could recover, Jerry and the real radio officers were on him, pinning him to the ground.

Within minutes, it was all over. Finch, the notorious Mr. Voice from the Cave, was in custody. A quick call to the hotel confirmed that his accomplice had indeed been caught on the roof, trying to dismantle a transmitter cleverly hidden inside a water tank. Jim McCoy was also taken into custody at the lighthouse.

As the sun began to rise over Sunset Beach, Jerry, Mrs. Deline, Penny, and Louise stood on the veranda of the Crystal Inn. The potted palms looked innocent in the morning light.

"You girls were incredibly brave," Mrs. Deline said, her voice losing its cold edge for the first time. "Especially you, Penny. Your imagination, which I confess I found irritating, is what truly solved this case."

"I guess my theories aren't always so wild," Penny said with a grin.

"Not always," Louise chuckled, looping an arm through her friend's. "But I'll still bet a cookie you'll have a new one by lunchtime."

Jerry smiled. "The FBI could use agents like you two. After you finish school, of course." He looked out at the calm sea. "Thanks to you, a very dangerous spy ring has been broken. You've done your country a great service."

Penny felt a thrill of pride. It had been a frightening and bewildering adventure, full of false clues and dangerous turns. But as she stood there with her best friend, watching the peaceful waves roll in, she knew it was a mystery she would never forget. And she had a feeling that their summer at Sunset Beach was far from over.

His gaze fell upon the carvings spread on the ground. "I thought you girls had gone," he said. "We... we're sorry," Penny stammered, feeling her face flush with shame. "They're beautiful," Louise said sincerely. "Truly." "Hmph," Jake grunted, but a faint touch of color came to his cheeks. "They're just whittling. But the wife... my Mary... she always liked them. She'd put them on the mantelpiece. Said they brought the sea into the house." He looked away, toward the cliff's edge. "She's gone five years now. The house gets... cluttered. Too many memories. So sometimes, I bring a few of the new ones up here. To give them a place to rest." The girls were silent. Penny's grand adventure had dissolved, replaced by a simple, human story. "We shouldn't have followed you," Penny said finally. "It was wrong of us. We'll help you put them back." The old man looked at the two girls, then at the carvings, and then back at the girls. A slow smile spread across his face, transforming his gruff features. "No," he said. "No, leave them out. The sun feels good on the wood." He nudged the little lighthouse with the toe of his boot. "Mary would have liked that one." He looked at Penny. "You've got a quick mind, girl. And a powerful imagination. You just point it in the right direction, and you'll be fine." He turned and walked away, not into the woods this time, but down the treacherous cliff path, moving with the sure-footedness of a man who had walked it his entire life. Penny and Louise carefully gathered up the carvings and placed them on a flat rock in the sun. The mystery of Jake Skagway was solved. It was not the mystery Penny had wanted, but she knew, somehow, it was a better one.

"And what about writing on her skirt?"

"I've been thinking about that," Penny said, stopping her pacing. "What if it wasn't invisible ink? What if it was something simpler? What if she was just tracing a pattern, or making an impression on a piece of paper she had underneath?"

"That's possible, I suppose," Louise conceded. "But we'll never know for sure."

"Maybe we will," Penny said, a new glint in her eye. She walked to the door and opened it a crack, peering out into the hallway. "Mrs. Deline's room is 214, just two doors down from us. We saw her go in there yesterday."

"Penny Parker, you are not to even think about going into her room!" Louise warned, sitting bolt upright. "That's breaking and entering!"

"Of course not," Penny said innocently. "I was just thinking. The maids will be turning down the beds soon. They leave the doors open while they work. We could just happen to be walking by."

"And do what? Walk right in and start searching her closets?"

"No! We'd just peek. See if there's anything interesting lying about. A map, a radio part, anything!"

Before Louise could protest further, they heard the tell-tale rattle of a service cart in the hallway. "It's now or never," Penny whispered, pulling Louise toward the door.

They slipped out into the corridor just as the maid, a tired looking woman with graying hair, pushed her cart to the door of room 214. She knocked once, and hearing no reply, unlocked it and went inside, leaving the door slightly ajar.

Penny and Louise sauntered past, trying to look as casual as possible. As they drew even with the open door, Penny pretended to stumble, catching herself on the doorframe. It gave her a perfect, unobstructed view of the room for a few precious seconds.

It was tidy, almost sterile. A suitcase lay open on a luggage rack, its contents neatly folded. The desk was clear except for a hotel notepad and a pen. A dark coat was draped over a chair. There was nothing that looked remotely suspicious. The maid was in the bathroom, running water.

"See? Nothing," Louise whispered, tugging Penny's sleeve. "Let's go."

Disappointed, Penny allowed herself to be pulled away. As she straightened up, her eyes fell upon the floor just outside the doorway. Lying on the patterned carpet was a small, crumpled piece of paper. It must have fallen when she bumped the door. Or perhaps it had been dropped earlier.

With a movement so quick Louise barely saw it, Penny bent down, scooped up the paper, and shoved it into her pocket. They hurried back to their room, and Penny closed the door firmly behind them.

"What was that? What did you pick up?" Louise demanded.

"I don't know yet," Penny said, her fingers trembling slightly as she pulled the wadded paper from her pocket. She carefully smoothed it out on the desk.

It was a small page, torn from a pocket-sized notebook. On it, written in neat, precise pencil, was a series of numbers and letters.

`TR-7`
`SW-14`
`NW-4`
`FENCE-2`

"What is it?" Louise breathed, peering over her shoulder.

"I don't know," Penny murmured, her eyes scanning the cryptic lines. "It looks like some kind of code. Or maybe directions."

"TR, SW, NW," Louise mused. "Those could be directions. Like southeast and northwest."

"But what about TR?" Penny wondered aloud. "And the numbers? Seven, fourteen, four, two."

"Look!" Louise exclaimed, pointing. "Fence! It says FENCE-2!"

Penny's eyes widened. "The drift fence! On the beach! Where Mrs. Deline buried the package!"

"It must be," Louise agreed, caught up in the excitement. "So it's a map of some kind! A map to the dune!"

"Of course!" Penny cried, slapping the desk. "This is what she was writing! She must have had this little notebook resting on her skirt and was writing down the location. This must have fallen out of her pocket later! She was making a map so her contact could find the spot!"

"But what do the directions mean?"

Penny stared at the paper, her brow furrowed in concentration. "Let's think. We were at the beach. She was near the dunes and the drift fence. TR-7. What could TR mean? And seven what? Seven feet? Seven paces?"

"Maybe TR stands for 'turn right'," Louise suggested.

"Good, Lou! That's good! So, turn right, seven paces. Then SW, southwest, fourteen paces. Then NW, northwest, four paces. That would lead you to a specific spot."

"And FENCE-2?"

"Maybe it means the second post of the fence? Or two paces from the fence?" Penny speculated. "We have to go back there. We have to try it!"

"Now?" Louise asked, glancing out the window. The sky was still overcast, but the rain had stopped. "It will be getting dark soon."

"All the better," Penny said grimly. "Fewer people to see us. We were fools to try digging in broad daylight. This time, we'll be more careful. We'll follow the map."

"But Penny, Mrs. Deline knows we were digging there. She'll be watching."

"That's why we won't go down the main steps. We'll go out the back of the hotel and cut across the lawn. She'll be looking for us on the veranda or the front beach, not sneaking around the side." Penny folded the piece of paper and tucked it securely in her pocket. "She may have scored on us once, but she won't do it again. Get your jacket, Louise. We're going to find out what's in that dune if it's the last thing we do."

Louise hesitated for only a moment. The thought of Jerry Livingston and the escaped prisoners was frightening, but the crumpled piece of paper in Penny's pocket was a tangible clue. It was proof that something was going on.

"All right," she said, a new resolve in her voice. "But if we see anyone, we run. Agreed?"

"Agreed," Penny said with a grin. "Let's go solve the mystery of the fish bones."

The girls slipped out a side door of the hotel and made their way toward the beach, keeping to the shadows of the building. The sand was cool and damp from the earlier rain. The sea was a churning slate gray, and a lonely looking fog was beginning to roll in, muffling the sound of the waves.

"This is spooky," Louise whispered, pulling her jacket tighter.

"It's perfect," Penny countered. "The fog will hide us."

They found the long, weathered drift fence that separated the wild dunes from the main part of the beach.

"Okay," Penny said, pulling out the note. "FENCE-2. What do you think it means?"

"Let's assume it means the second fence post from the north end," Louise suggested, always practical. They paced along the fence until they reached the second splintered post.

"Right," Penny said, her voice filled with nervous energy. "Now, TR-7. Turn right, seven paces." She stood with her back to the fence post and took seven deliberate steps into the shifting sands of the dune area. "Here. Now, SW-14. Southwest." She squinted, trying to get her bearings in the fading light. "That way."

She carefully paced off fourteen steps, her shoes sinking into the soft sand. Louise followed close behind.

"Now what?"

"NW-4. Northwest, four paces," Penny read. She turned again and took four more steps, ending up in a small hollow between two marram grass-covered dunes. "This has to be the place."

It looked no different from any other spot in the vast, rolling landscape of sand. But according to the map, this was it.

"Well?" Louise prompted. "Are you going to dig?"

"I don't have a shovel," Penny said, realizing the flaw in her plan. She looked around frantically, then her eyes lit up. On the side of the dune, half-buried in sand, was a large, flat piece of driftwood. "This will have to do."

Using the wood as a makeshift spade, Penny began to scrape away at the damp sand. It was slow, tiring work. Louise joined in, using her hands to scoop the sand that Penny loosened. They dug in silence for several minutes, the only sounds the scraping of the wood and the distant sigh of the ocean.

"Maybe your directions were wrong," Louise panted, pausing to rest.

"They can't be," Penny insisted, digging with renewed vigor. "We followed them exactly."

Her piece of driftwood hit something hard. It wasn't the dull thud of a rock. It was a hollow, metallic sound.

"I've found it!" she gasped. "I've found it, Lou!"

Working together, they frantically cleared the remaining sand away from the object. It was a small, tin box, about the size of a loaf of bread, painted a dull gray. It was heavier than it looked. A simple clasp held the lid shut.

"Open it!" Louise urged, her eyes wide.

Penny's fingers fumbled with the cold metal clasp. It was stiff, but with a final grunt of effort, she pried it open. She lifted the lid.

Inside, nestled in a bed of cotton wool, was not a secret radio part, or a roll of microfilm, or a bundle of money. It was a collection of seashells.

They were beautiful, intricate shells of all shapes and sizes. There was a delicate pink scallop, a perfectly spiraled whelk, a pearly white sand dollar, and a dozen smaller, common shells arranged carefully around them.

Penny stared, utterly baffled. "Seashells?"

"Just seashells?" Louise echoed in disbelief.

Penny lifted the cotton batting. There was nothing underneath. She picked up the tin box and shook it. Nothing rattled. It was just a box of seashells.

"I don't understand," Penny said, her voice a mixture of frustration and confusion. "All this secrecy. The map. The lies. For a box of shells?"

"Maybe they're very rare shells," Louise offered weakly.

"Rare enough to be part of an enemy spy ring?" Penny retorted. She sank back on her heels, the empty tin box in her lap. The grand conspiracy she had so carefully constructed had crumbled into a pile of sand and ordinary shells. Mrs. Deline had made a fool of her not once, but twice.

A sudden noise made them both freeze. It was the sound of a footstep on the sand, very close by.

Before they could react, a dark figure loomed over them out of the fog.

"I believe you have something that belongs to me."

The voice was cold, sharp, and unmistakable. It was Mrs. Deline.
